section_judgments.section_text_excerpt: In 1057, the ecclesiastical reformer Peter Damian (d. 1072/3) explained in a letter to his fellow cardinal bishops how a lump of debased silver might be remade into different coins but still remain a dangerous forgery, in the same way as a corrupt priest would always be tainted by his abuses.1 The image was presum- ably effective, for the same author used similar monetary meta- phors on several other occasions. By doing so he tapped into a long Christian tradition developed in the Bible and subsequently in the writings of Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory the Great and others.2 But in the ﬁve centuries between the age of Gregory and that of Peter Damian, monetary metaphors were very rarely called on.3 A revealing exception comes in Bede’s Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum. The saintly princess Eorcengota at one point dreams of angelic men in white scouring her monastery in search of a ‘gold coin’ (aureum . . . nomisma) brought there from Kent, by which Bede meant Eorcengota herself.4 In this case the coin was gold, and clearly signiﬁed something of rare interest and value. section_judgments.notes: Brief but substantive outline of how precious-metal coinage depends on bullion supply channels (recycling, reminting, imports, mining). Useful comparative context for monetization constraints.
section_judgments.section_text_excerpt: RIVERS OF GOLD AND SILVER: COINAGE AND Any coinage based on precious metal relied on a supply of gold or silver to exist. Minting authorities could obtain this bullion in four principal ways: recycling the local currency; melting down domestic stocks of gold or silver in other forms; reminting precious metals coming in from other terri- tories; and fresh extraction from mines. This last was com- paratively rare: a point which lies behind one of the fundamental attractions of precious metal throughout history. Gold and silver were suitable for currency precisely because they existed in restricted quantity, which meant that supply was likely to be uneven and constantly in ﬂux. Great rivers of gold and silver ﬂowing across seas and frontiers have glit- tered brightly in the past, dominating interpretations of mon- etary development and ﬁguring prominently in views of interregional exchange. Fernand Braudel wrote of the ‘swelling currents’ of gold and silver that criss-crossed the Atlantic and the Mediterranean in the sixteenth century as one of many phenomena characterized by ‘slow but perceptible rhythms’.15

This move was mirrored in what were essentially monetary appendages of Merovingian Gaul: England and Frisia.18 The end result was the establishment of a northern monetary zone, centred on the Frankish king- dom and its silver coins — a zone which would remain a co- herent and powerful force for centuries to come. section_judgments.notes: Appears to duplicate the start of the following subsection ('From gift to market...'); provides some context on local coin circulation but is structurally noisy as a separate section.
section_judgments.section_text_excerpt: FROM GIFT TO MARKET AND KING TO PEASANT: COINAGE IN If large-scale movement and development of currency was essen- tially the sum of local transactions, the beating heart of early medieval monetization was to be found in day-to-day life within individual towns, villages and households. Zooming in to this level requires tighter chronological and geographical focus: effectively on to the Carolingian empire from the late eighth cen- tury onwards, and on to contemporary Anglo-Saxon England. These are maximal cases for early medieval Europe. Both present comparative economic and administrative sophistication, and above all rich numismatic and written sources, which make them models of how far the monetary economy could develop. Even so, both contained patches of more and less dense coin use, as well as established routes for travel and exchange. In the Carolingian empire, northern and central Italy remained distinct from each other and from the areas across the Alps. Northern Francia, from approximately the Loire to theRhine, saw generally rich circulation as an accompaniment to elaborate local ex- change, while Aquitaine contained several comparatively isolated pockets of circulation.65 Southern and eastern England were probably comparable to northern Francia in the vibrancy of their monetary economy by the later seventh century. There, growth in coin circulation took place alongside broadening pro- duction and distribution of ceramics, most famously Ipswich ware, and also rising aristocratic and ecclesiastical wealth.66

section_ref.section_title: ELITES, PEASANTS AND THE POWER OF CURRENCY

section_judgments.notes: Useful comparative discussion of how elites and estate networks shape surplus extraction, redistribution, and the intensity of monetized exchange; indirect relevance to Roman-to-post-Roman economic transformation.
section_judgments.section_text_excerpt: ELITES, PEASANTS AND THE POWER OF CURRENCY At the core of any assessment of the effect of currency in early medieval society has to be the role of those with greatest wealth: secular and ecclesiastical landowning elites.113 This is more than 111 Wickham,Framing the Early MiddleAges,674–92;Naismith,MoneyandPower in Anglo-Saxon England, 255–8. 112 Spufford, Money and its Use in Medieval Europe, 382–6; Mick Reed, ‘‘‘Gnawing it Out’’: a New Look at Economic Relations in Nineteenth-Century Rural England’, Rural History, i (1990), esp. 84–5. 113 Wickham, ‘Rethinking’, 22–4; Devroey, ‘Re´ﬂexions sur l’e´conomie des prem- iers temps carolingiens’, 476–81; see also above, n. 108. THE SOCIAL SIGNIFICANCE OF MONETIZATION an early medieval incarnation of Reaganomics. Landand its prod- ucts were fundamental to serious mobilization of resources, and consequently those with large territorial holdings occupied a pri- vileged position. Other sources of moveable wealth — commerce and specialized production, for example — were signiﬁcant, but a poor second overall. Areas characterized by highly developed net- works of bulk exchange and heaviest use of coin also tended to possess particularly wealthy elites with numerous estates and well-articulated methods for extracting surplus from them. Thanks to the preferential survival of Church sources these are the institutions about which most is known. Canterbury cath- edral already in the eighth century had extensive landholdings as far aﬁeld as Buckinghamshire and Oxfordshire,114 while sev- eral Carolingian monasteries of the ninth century had networks of transport and communication to tend interests spanning hun- dreds of kilometres.115 Much could thereby have been dispensed to or retained by dependants at various levels without any com- mercial exchange ever taking place. But by redistributing goods across estates and marshalling agricultural commodities in bulk, elites had the potential to build up reserves, support production and drive exchange on a comparatively signiﬁcant scale, from which other segments of society could beneﬁt indirectly. section_judgments.notes: Synthesizes the argument that local market-driven exchange, not just bullion flows or elite/state structures, drives coin circulation; useful for broad framing but not directly about the late Roman West.
section_judgments.section_text_excerpt: The heartbeat of the early medieval monetary economy did not solely follow the resonant thumps of large-scale ﬂows of bullion, or indeed the clearer rhythms generated by elite or state power structures. It developed most intensively when in sync with a 142 Ibid., 85–91, 94. 143 Metcalf, Atlas of Anglo-Saxon and Norman Coin Finds, 14–101; Naismith, ‘English Monetary Economy’; Naismith, ‘London and its Mint’. 144 Fleming, ‘Rural Elites and Urban Communities’. 145 David Hill, ‘Trends in the Development of Towns during the Reign of Ethelred II’, in David Hill (ed.), Ethelred the Unready: Papers from the Millenary Conference (Oxford, 1978), 217–25. 146 Naismith, ‘Gold Coinage and its Use’. lower-level hum of activity: networks of market-driven, commer- cial exchange which formed the background noise of monetized exchange. Movement of gold and silver across borders and seas did not by itself dictate the metal or type of coinage in use. Rather, this movement reﬂects the sum of all other transactions and re- lations writ large: bullion supply was as much a result as a cause of monetary changes. It follows that the driving forces behind use and circulation of currency were concentrated at a more local level, tapping into the livesofpeasantsaswell as merchants and elites.Thiswasnot just a matter of gift-giving — though monetary gifts certainly existed — nor indeed just of coin. There must always have been a healthy background of non-monetized exchange, sufﬁciently prevalent that even quite large ﬂuctuations in the size of the currency had a limited effect on prices. Rather, the greatest demand for mon- etization lay in more ‘neutral’ interactions such as buying and selling. Coinage was most closely associated with those who engaged in such transactions, and areas where these and other manifestations of economic complexity were strongest were where monetary exchange emerges as most important. Nevertheless, economic relations remained intensely per- sonal even in areas of greatest complexity, and so an inevitable consequence of the developing role of currency was its em- broilment with social interactions in complex and often dan- gerous ways.
